opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of virtual worlds and the physical world as two ends of one continuum, and the most interesting robotics work sits right between them.

The core problem in robotics is data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Robots have nothing comparable. You can't scrape motor commands off the web. Collecting real-world robot data through teleoperation is valuable, but it's slow and expensive, and it's capped by how many human-hours and how many physical robots you have. Fundamentally, it doesn't scale the way we need.

That's where virtual worlds come in. In simulation, you can run thousands of environments in parallel on GPUs, faster than real time. You can randomize physics, lighting, textures, object shapes, and friction, so the policy you train has seen so much variety that the real world looks like just another variation. That's the idea behind sim-to-real transfer. If your simulator is diverse enough, reality becomes one more sample from the distribution.

I like to think of it as a data pyramid with three layers.

- **Base: internet-scale data.** Videos and text of humans doing things. It gives you common sense and priors about how the world works, but it has no action labels.
- **Middle: synthetic data.** This comes from classical physics simulation, and increasingly from generative models. Video world models can now "dream" plausible futures, so a model can, in a sense, simulate a world it has never physically touched.
- **Tip: real robot data.** It's the scarcest and most precious layer. It grounds everything and closes the final gap.

So the relationship is complementary, not competitive. The physical world is the ground truth and the final exam. Virtual worlds are where you do most of the studying. The more we can convert compute into data, through simulation and world models, the less we're bottlenecked by atoms.

There's also a deeper point here. I believe the virtual and the physical will eventually share a single model. A robot foundation model that understands physics well enough to act in reality should also be able to imagine and simulate reality. Prediction and action are two sides of the same coin. When we get there, the boundary between simulating a world and acting in one gets very thin.

r001.rationale: It calls virtual and physical worlds “two ends of one continuum” and says the physical world is ground truth, but does not clearly frame them as ultimately different realities along a single axis.

r002.rationale: It describes randomizing simulated physics and other properties so a policy trains across varied simulated environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I actually think of virtual worlds and the physical world as a single continuum rather than two separate things, and the whole arc of my work has been about moving along that continuum.

I started in games, with Minecraft agents like MineDojo and Voyager. At the time people would ask, why Minecraft, isn't that a toy? But a game is really just a physics engine plus a reward structure, and it gave us an open-ended world where an agent could explore, build tools, and learn skills with essentially unlimited data. The lesson there was that if you have a rich simulator, you can train very general agents, because you're never data-starved.

Robotics is the opposite problem. The physical world is the ultimate environment, but data is incredibly expensive. Every trajectory costs real time, real hardware, sometimes a broken gripper. There's no internet of robot actions the way there's an internet of text. So the natural move is to bring the virtual-world playbook over: build simulators good enough that most of the learning happens there, and then close the gap to reality.

That's what we're doing with Project GR00T and the simulation stack at NVIDIA. We use GPU-accelerated physics to run thousands of environments in parallel, so a humanoid can experience years of practice in hours. We use generative models to randomize textures, lighting, object shapes, so the policy never overfits to one particular rendering of the world. And increasingly we use world models, essentially learned simulators, that can predict what happens next from video, which blurs the line even further. A good enough world model is a virtual world you didn't have to hand-build.

The way I'd put it: the virtual world is where the robot gets its education, and the physical world is where it takes the exam. The craft is making the education look enough like the exam that the robot doesn't notice it's been transferred. And I think the trajectory is toward a point where real data, synthetic data, and simulation are all just blended inputs to one foundation model, and the distinction between virtual and physical stops being something we even talk about.

r001.rationale: It describes virtual and physical worlds as “a single continuum” and as movement along that continuum, framing them as different points on one axis.

r002.rationale: It mentions randomizing textures, lighting, and object shapes in simulation, but does not describe varying physical parameters across simulated worlds.

astra-6.text:
I think of virtual worlds as a training ground for intelligence that ultimately has to work in the physical world. In simulation, a robot can practice a skill over and over, make mistakes safely, and encounter a much wider range of situations than we could easily set up in a lab. You can run many of those experiences in parallel, which is really important for scaling learning.

But simulation is always an approximation. Contact, friction, the way an object deforms—those things can be difficult to model. So the question is: how do you learn something in a virtual world that remains useful when those details change? One approach is to vary the simulated conditions so the robot learns a robust skill instead of memorizing one environment.

The physical world is the ultimate test. You bring the policy onto a real robot, see where it fails, and use those failures to improve the training. So I see the two as a feedback loop: virtual worlds give us scale, and the physical world keeps us grounded.

r001.rationale: It presents simulation and the physical world as a training-and-feedback loop, but does not frame them as different realities along a single axis.

r002.rationale: It describes varying simulated conditions, including contact and friction, so the robot learns a robust skill across differing physical parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of virtual worlds as a training ground for intelligence that can eventually operate in the physical world. A robot needs a tremendous amount of experience, and collecting all of that experience on real hardware is slow. In simulation, you can run many environments in parallel, let the robot fail safely, and expose it to a wide range of situations.

But the relationship goes both ways. The physical world tells us where our simulations are wrong. You train a policy virtually, test it on a real robot, and use those failures to improve the next round of training. The goal isn’t a perfect digital copy of everything. It’s to capture enough of what matters that the robot learns skills that transfer—and can adapt when reality surprises it.

r001.rationale: It describes simulation as a training ground and the physical world as a test and feedback source, but does not frame them as different realities along a single axis.

r002.rationale: It mentions varied situations in simulation, but does not describe varying physical parameters or identify this as domain randomization.
